title: NYC ballot proposals: What the 5 questions mean for voters on Election Day 2026 - ABC7 New York

NYC ballot proposals: What the 5 questions mean for voters on Election Day 2026 - ABC7 New York 
 24/7 Live New York City New Jersey Long Island Northern Suburbs Connecticut POLITICS 
 What to know about the 5 ballot questions for New York City voters 
 Friday, October 30, 2026 6:39PM 
 Mike Marza explains what the ballots questions are and what they could mean for New Yorkers. Adobe Stock NEW YORK (WABC) -- As early voting gets underway in New York on Saturday, New York City residents will also be asked to answer five ballot questions.
 Here are the ballot questions and what they could mean for New Yorkers:
 1. Speed up Process for Outdoor Dining
 This measure would simplify the process for using public space for things like ramps, planters and cafes by removing mandatory hearings.
 A yes vote would speed up the process for getting permission for outdoor space, such as restaurant dining. A no vote maintains the longer process with a mandatory public hearing to use public space and a Council review of sidewalk cafes.
 2. Reduce Paperwork for City Contractors
 The second ballot question would reduce paperwork for city contractors.
 A yes vote will amend the Procurement Policy Board authority and authorize the mayor to delegate certain contract approvals. A no vote leaves laws unchanged, with the mayor and comptroller maintaining a longer questionnaire.
 3. Streamline Process for Bike And Bus Lanes
 The third question aims to streamline the process for adding bike and bus lanes by simplifying the review of street safety projects. It would also expedite leasing offices for city workforce use.
 A yes vote will simplify street project approval, city property disposition and office leasing. Voting no will maintain intra-agency consultation for road projects, Council approval for city property dispositions and Council disapproval of office leases.
 4. Simplify Construction Permitting Process
 The fourth question would simplify the construction permitting process and move waterfront permitting from the Department of Small Business Services to the Department of Buildings.
 A yes vote authorizes a centralized permit hub, and a no vote leaves the law unchanged.
 5. Set Target for Reserve Funds
 This measure sets a target amount of money to hold in reserve funds, including a rainy day fund.
 A yes vote requires the mayor to develop a method for calculating deposits to the fund, while a no vote leaves the law unchanged.
